Computational Thinking

Unit 1 • Standard Level • Year 12

2 Weeks (6 Lessons)

The Big Question

"How do we take a messy, real-world problem and turn it into something a computer can solve?"

This unit teaches you Computational Thinking — a powerful problem-solving toolkit. You'll learn how to transform "wicked" messy problems into clear, structured solutions using four key pillars: Abstraction, Decomposition, Pattern Recognition, and Algorithmic Thinking.

What You'll Learn

  • B1.1.1 — Problem Specification

    Before writing any code, you need to truly understand the problem. You'll learn to identify:

    • Stakeholders — Who is affected by this problem?
    • Problem Statement — What exactly are we trying to solve?
    • Inputs & Outputs — What goes in, what comes out?
    • Constraints — What limitations do we have?
    • Success Criteria — How will we know if our solution works?
  • B1.1.2 & B1.1.3 — The Four Pillars of Computational Thinking
    🔍 Abstraction

    Removing unnecessary detail to focus on what matters. Like the London Tube Map — it ignores real geography to show connections clearly.

    🧩 Decomposition

    Breaking a complex problem into smaller, manageable parts. Like building IKEA furniture — tackle one step at a time.

    🔄 Pattern Recognition

    Spotting similarities and repeating structures. If you've solved something similar before, you can reuse that logic.

    📋 Algorithmic Thinking

    Designing step-by-step instructions that can be followed precisely. Every step must be clear and unambiguous.

  • B1.1.4 — Flowcharts & Trace Tables

    You'll learn to represent algorithms visually using standard flowchart symbols, and test them using "dry runs" with trace tables — tracking how variables change step by step.

Watch Out For These Mistakes

❌ "Decomposition means breaking down code"

Decomposition happens before you write any code. You break down the problem into smaller parts, not the program. You can decompose a problem without ever touching a computer.

❌ "Abstraction makes things more complicated"

Abstraction is the opposite — it means removing irrelevant details to make things simpler. Think of a map: it abstracts away trees, buildings, and street names to show you just what you need.

❌ Flowchart mistakes

Always label your decision branches with Yes/No or True/False. Never leave flowlines disconnected or dangling — every path must lead somewhere (either another step or a terminator).

Thinking Deeper

These are the kinds of questions that connect this unit to bigger ideas about knowledge and thinking:

  • "The map is not the territory"

    When we abstract, we create a simplified model of reality. The London Tube Map deliberately distorts geography to make connections clearer. What do we gain from this simplification? What do we lose?

  • Does naming a problem limit our solutions?

    When we write a problem specification, we categorise and define the problem. Does this help us find solutions, or does it "freeze" our thinking into predetermined paths?
